title: Douglass on two Christianities
hook: Frederick Douglass rejected slaveholders' religion and loved the Christianity of Christ

segments.voice: Yesterday: Harriet Tubman, who reached freedom and turned around to go back. Your line was the moses of her people.

The last page is written. It's the story of a life in slavery, told by the man who lived it, sharp and angry and full of church people: an enslaver who got religion at a camp meeting and became crueler afterward, a man who led prayers in his house and used the whip in his fields. The author reads it over and realizes a reader might think he hates religion altogether. So he adds a few more pages at the very end, to make himself clear: hard words about the church, from a man who loved Christ. Today: Frederick Douglass, on two Christianities.
screen: `A FEW PAGES ADDED AT THE END.`

segments.voice: Douglass had escaped slavery and become a speaker against it. In his Narrative, he tells what he saw: enslavers who were church members, even preachers, and no kinder for it. He writes that the religious slaveholders he knew were the worst of all. So in the appendix he says plainly what he meant: "between the Christianity of this land, and the Christianity of Christ, I recognize the widest possible difference." And: "I love the pure, peaceable, and impartial Christianity of Christ." Hear those three words against the slaveholding religion he describes. Pure: not mixed with profit. Peaceable: not backed by the whip. Impartial: not taking sides by the color of someone's skin. The other kind, the slaveholding religion, he says he hates with the same force. He wasn't attacking faith from the outside. He was making a distinction from the inside, the way the prophets did. Scripture offers a test of its own. The letter of James says, in the King James Bible: "Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction." Set that beside one of Douglass's words for the slaveholders' religion: "cradle-plundering." A faith that cares for orphans and a faith that takes children from their mothers can sing the same hymns on Sunday. For Douglass, they were still not the same faith. He leaves a hard question for any believer, in any century: which Christianity is mine?

Bring to mind something you do in the name of what you believe, or of being a good person: a habit, a cause, a way you treat people. Hold it up against his three words: is it pure, peaceable, impartial? Don't punish yourself, just look honestly, and if you pray, ask to see clearly.
Frederick Douglass. The escaped former slave whose narrative named two Christianities, the slaveholders' religion and the pure, peaceable Christianity of Christ he loved.
Your line: the christianity of christ. Pure, peaceable, impartial: his test fits in a pocket. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Christians read Douglass's appendix in churches, classes and seminaries as a test of their own faith, sometimes alongside the prophets and the letter of James.
